description:
We have exams next week so naturally we’re planning a trip to Mars.

We’re three tech students from Norway into coding, AI and making cool stuff. Taking on the Martian Map challenge with NASA data, 3D visuals and a questionable sense of priorities. Hopefully better at navigating Mars than planning our semester.
summary:
What if the most exciting discovery on Mars came from our own glove?

Clean Approach helps astronauts plan rock sampling near Bright Angel, Mars. It combines real NASA terrain data and sample documentation with an illustrative activity plan, showing how gloves, tools and surfaces can connect to a sample’s contact history.

Users explore the map, compare handling choices and trace possible contact pathways, not measured contamination. The goal is to help explorers understand what their own activities might introduce before interpreting a discovery.

Find Mars. Not ourselves.
details:
Finding something interesting on Mars is only half the challenge. Understanding whether we brought it with us is the other half.

Clean Approach is an interactive planning prototype for astronauts collecting rock samples near Bright Angel, Mars. It connects a geographic terrain map with a sample’s contact history: which gloves, tools and surfaces could have contributed material before the sample was sealed?

How it works

The interface guides users through three steps: Mission, Plan and Sample history. Users explore the terrain, review an illustrative sampling plan and inspect the connections created by its handling events.

An event-based graph tracks possible source histories through assumed contacts. Each event updates the history associated with the objects involved. Sealing a sample preserves its history at that moment; explicitly reopening it allows subsequent contacts to affect that history. Changing a handling assumption changes the connections shown.

This makes a subtle problem visible: separate equipment does not automatically mean an independent sample history. What matters is the complete sequence of contacts.

NASA data and scientific context

We combine Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX terrain and imagery, distributed through USGS, with Perseverance sample documentation from NASA’s Planetary Data System. CTX provides geographic context; the Sapphire Canyon sample documentation provides the scientific context for the Bright Angel scenario.

Terrain is rendered with horizontal and vertical dimensions in meters, and missing data remains visible as gaps. The sample marker uses a nominal documented coordinate, not a verified drilling position. Astronaut activities and contact events are explicitly illustrative.

What makes it different

A conventional route map shows where an astronaut goes. Clean Approach also asks what history a sample acquires along the way. Linking these two views makes sample integrity part of mission planning rather than something considered only after collection.

The intended benefit is to help users identify handling assumptions, compare alternatives and understand why documenting sample history matters when interpreting scientific results.

Technology and scope

The application uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Canvas-based terrain rendering, Python geospatial data preparation and static hosting through GitHub Pages. The presentation video was created with Remotion. AI coding tools supported development, debugging and documentation.

The prototype models possible connections, not measured contamination, transfer quantities or biological survival. Its purpose is to make those connections inspectable—not to certify an astronaut procedure as safe.

Find Mars. Not ourselves.
